catalog_quote: Several writers have indicated that Dangme monosyllables carry a system of three contrastive tones. ... The present writer has also maintained that the primary contrast is between high and non-high. That is, in a series of two or more syllables, the contrast between mids and lows on successive syllables is commonly neutralized, but the contrast between either of these and high tone is almost always maintained. ... In other words, on syllables in final position, there is a three term tonal system, high, mid and low, each of the three terms being fully contrastive with each of the others. This three term system also obtains on syllables immediately preceding a high tone. On syllables preceding a non-high tone, however, there is only a two-term system of contrast, high and non-high. sweep_summary: search for Adangme/Dangme (adan1247, catalog classification tonal, deciding source Kropp Dakubu 1974 JWAL 9(2), already read first-hand by our earlier reading). The target list held exactly one title-keyword hit, Riney & Flege 1998 (SSLA), whose Crossref abstract (saved) shows it is a study of global foreign accent in Japanese learners of English -- not Dangme, not word stress; the noise flag is correct and the link to adan1247 is a Glottolog mis-tagging (it is absent from the saved Glottolog langdoc JSON for adan1247). Supplementary open-source probes turned up nothing new: archive.org title/subject search for Dangme/Adangme returns only the Rosetta Project excerpts of Kropp Dakubu 1987 (consonant/vowel pages, no stress passage; already held by the project) and Bibles; the already-saved Caesar & Sackitey 2024 'Elision in Dangme' text has no occurrence of 'stress'/'accent'; Semantic Scholar could not be reached by automated download; No first-hand stress statement was newly read in this search of works with stress in the title, so no new stress statement was found and the catalog's current deciding source stands unchallenged.

tone_statements.citation: Kropp, Mary Esther. 1968. A comparative study of Gã and Adangme with special reference to the verb. PhD thesis, University of London (SOAS). 329 pp. (Glottolog ref 573747)
tone_statements.quote: Whereas Ga has two contrastive levels of level pitch sequences, Adangme has three. … The facts described in >#• 2 can be accounted for in terms of two tone phonemes in Ga; high, marked', and low, unmarked or \ thre&^in Adangme; high, marked mid, marked -, and low, V| or unmarked, and downstep, marked ', which is a phonemic tonal juncture phenomenon. … Ga has two contrastive single pitch levels of utterance; Adangme has three. As a result, Ga is analyzed in terms of two tones, Adangme 'in terms , of three.
tone_statements.locator: p.77 (1.4.2.23 Level Pitch Sequences; 1.4.3 The Phonemes) and p.86 (1.4.6 Conclusions); TBU statement p.44 (1.1.1), 'every syllable.. carries phonemic tone' p.73 (1.4.2)
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones, high, mid and low, on every syllable, plus downstep (terraced-level system); falls analysed as two syllables; low/mid and mid/downstepped-high alternations; nothing on stress.

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim on the page scan of the held primary (Dakubu 1974:79) and the held secondary (Adomako 2018:19). The deciding source is a dedicated tone article by the principal authority on Dangme, and an independent open 2024 phonology article (Caesar & Sackitey, downloaded now, pp.5-6) restates the same three-level contrastive register-tone system with the syllable as domain and never mentions stress. Glottolog has no full reference grammar for Dangme; the 130-pp Kropp Dakubu 1987 survey and Apronti 1967 PhD remain unheld but everything reachable (their content as relayed by Adomako 2018 and Caesar & Sackitey 2024, plus Rosetta excerpts) is consistent with tonal, domain not stated by the source. No database (StressTyp2/WALS) values exist to contradict. Bibliographic searches (CrossRef, UGSpace, UEW repository, archive.org; web search/OpenAlex/S2 budgets exhausted) surfaced no work asserting Dang

sources.quote: 'Finally, Dangme, like other Kwa languages such as Akan and Ewe, is a register tone language. It has three level tones, which are contrastive. The three level tones in Dangme are high as in /má/ 'dough' mid as in /mā/ 'herrings' and low as in /mà/ 'town'.' (pp.5-6). The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the 38 pages; no accent/prominence statement.
